Want to understand how the market feels about a company’s debt? 

Look at its yield spread over comparable Treasuries.

That’s the extra yield investors demand to lend to that company.

Examples from http://TreasuryBonds.com for bonds maturing in November 2036:

• Microsoft: +0.60 percentage points
• Meta: +1.46 percentage points

Investors demand more than twice the extra yield to hold Meta’s debt.

Wider spreads generally signal greater perceived credit risk, though liquidity and bond terms also matter.

Search a company and check “Spread vs. Treasury” at http://TreasuryBonds.com.

text:
The bears are having their moment.

After predicting a top in the AI trade every month for the last 4 years, the bears finally got their moment last week.

However, in 3 to 6 months, we are going to look back at this correction and realize it was just that: a correction.

There is a widespread narrative right now that Nvidia, $NVDA, is quite literally going to collapse. This is a stock that was trading at a record high on October 6th, worth nearly $6 trillion, and the inventor of the most advanced chips in the world (it's not even close).

That's how deeply pessimistic sentiment has become over the last seven weeks.

Even if Nvidia produced half as much revenue as they are guiding for their next fiscal year, this company would still produce close to $400 billion in annual revenue.

Meanwhile, the S&P 500 has posted three consecutive quarters with earnings growth above 25% and eight straight quarters of double-digit growth.

And, sentiment flipped so quickly that the S&P 500 closed the week 4.1 standard deviations below its 50-day moving average on Friday. Not even 2020 and 2008 saw such an occurrence.

The reality is that AI truly is the "next big thing" and the AI buildout is only accelerating.

Bears will sound smart, bulls will make money.

Is there a fix for $BTC's quantum risk?

Ran Neuner sees a quantum threat in the foreseeable future and doesn't think anyone will save Bitcoin, because its devs can't agree on a solution

"I hate saying it because I think Bitcoin did start this industry, but it doesn't excite me anymore."

"I do hold a lot of Bitcoin and I hold them as an insurance policy and because I'm emotionally attached to them. I don't say I don't like the Bitcoin thesis, because I do."

"Technology is moving very fast. At some point there's going to be a technological risk to Bitcoin."

"When that technological risk happens, I don't believe that there's going to be anyone to save us. Quantum computing is the risk in the foreseeable future."

"I've seen these Bitcoin devs. I've seen them trying to coordinate. It's worse than when my kids order pizza."

"They can't decide what pizza they want. This one wants olives, this one wants cheese. That's how the Bitcoin devs are when it comes to quantum."

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has completely changed his view on Nvidia, $NVDA, over the last 7 days.

“Well, Jensen is on the outside now.”

When pressed on whether Jensen Huang should return, Bessent said, “I think we have to see where the buck stops,” clearly leaving the door open.

Is there still a thesis for holding $ETH and $SOL?

Ran Neuner says he isn't bullish on L1s yet and prefers protocols like Hyperliquid and Backpack, with real, growing revenue that flows back to token holders

"I don't like the layer 1 thesis at all. In order for a token to have value, it's either going to be really scarce, or it's going to have a way of paying dividends or money to its holders."

"If you think about ETH or SOL, they're not really scarce assets, because they just keep minting more. They don't have a buyback program, or they don't give any money back to the holder."

"I'm not really bullish layer 1s yet, but I am bullish things on top of the layer 1s, where they do have the correct economics."

"I'm bullish on things like Hyperliquid. I'm bullish on a protocol called Backpack."

"It's got to have a real use case. It's got to have real and growing users, with real and growing revenue. And then it's got to have a way of giving value back to the token holders."

text:
Very bad advice: PEG is a tool for steady compounders. For cyclicals, you look at where you are in the cycle—normalized/mid-cycle earnings, price-to-book, capacity, inventory, spreads—not a growth multiple that flatters the peak and punishes the trough. Using PEG on a cyclical is like judging a rollercoaster by its average height: technically true, practically useless.  PEG doesn't work for cyclicals because it assumes earnings growth is smooth and predictable—cyclical earnings are neither.
 
Here's the simple version:
• PEG = P/E ÷ growth rate. It's designed for companies whose earnings grow steadily year after year (like software or consumer staples). A low PEG is supposed to mean "cheap growth."
• Cyclical earnings swing wildly—autos, steel, airlines, semis, energy. In a boom, earnings spike and the P/E looks low. In a bust, earnings collapse and the P/E looks high (or goes negative).
• So PEG gets it backwards. At the top of the cycle, when the stock is actually most dangerous, trailing growth looks great and PEG looks cheap. At the bottom, when the stock may be cheapest, earnings are troughing, growth looks terrible, and PEG looks expensive—or meaningless.
• The "G" is unreliable. A cyclical's growth rate over the past few years tells you almost nothing about the next few, because it's driven by the cycle, not by a durable compounding engine. You're dividing by a number that's about to reverse.

en_summary: Sees bearish takedown of AI and neoclouds making rounds. Agrees standing massive AI datacenters is hard and capital harder, but notes self-interest. Owns $SPCX, believes it may be largest AI hyperscaler soon, amazing execution. Also positions in $IREN and $CRWV. Crushing NEOs in best interest of Elon and SpaceX for pricing power etc. SpaceX still plans tens of GW. Conditions real but creating spiral for smaller AI clouds in his interest. text:
I see this one making the rounds as some bearish takedown of AI and in particular neoclouds.

1. He’s right that standing these massive AI datacenters is extremely hard. 
2. Yes, capital is harder to come by and will present a challenge for some companies.
3. He’s not a disinterested third party providing a viewpoint. 

I own $SPCX and believe it may be the largest AI hyperscaler in the not too distant future. Amazing execution. I also have positions in $IREN and $CRWV. 

But, let’s not pretend that there is no self interest here. Crushing the NEOs is absolutely in the best interest of Elon and SpaceX here. Better for pricing power, capital allocation, margins, customer acquisition, and so on and so forth. 

Note SpaceX still plans to stand up 10s of GW in short order because it is really good business for the company. The less competition the better. 

So two things can be true at the same time. The conditions Elon speaks to are real, but creating a massive spiral for smaller AI clouds is definitely in his best interest. It’s good use of the platform and a good chess move. But it isn’t just some altruistic advice for investors. 

Carry on.

Good observation on the dilution risks with $IREN. 

The dilution has been pretty bad looking backwards. It wouldn’t be that big of a concern if mgmt didn’t top themselves up for that dilution. It creates a fundamental misalignment between management and shareholders and reeks of poor corporate governance. 

The flip side of that coin is that the Roberts brothers will lose meaningful say in the company if they get diluted and we don’t want that either. These two are the visionaries behind the company and the engine behind its growth. If massively diluted, they either get distracted by other endeavours or other investors jump in and drive the governance from the boarded level. 

A catch 22. 

That is why, in specific circumstances like the one IREN is in, with a steep growth curve ahead of it, mgmt top-ups are a necessary evil. 

But, as a private markets investor, it’s a tough pill for me to swallow. 

As for $NUAI, it doesn’t fit in the same conversation as IREN just yet. NUAI is a different risk profile altogether until they sign a tenant.

All that said, both companies are dirt cheap. Do the napkin math on what a fully leased MW generates in revenue (under either business model) today vs the cost of create said revenue and you’ll find these investments very compelling. 

Overthink it and you miss the opportunity.

en_summary: FSD v15 is starting to hit cars today, and I think this is a really BIG one. Elon says wider release coming in December with holiday update, calling it something special. First wave. Tesla says 25x better handling of safety critical cases, release notes describe 25x improvement in critical intervention rate.
text:
FSD v15 is starting to hit cars today, and I think this is a really BIG one.

Elon says the wider release is coming in December with the holiday update, calling it “something special.” This is the first wave, so if your car hasn’t received it yet, that’s normal fyi. 

The number everyone’s going to talk about is 25x.

Tesla says it's “25x better handling of safety critical cases,” while the release notes describe a 25x improvement in the critical intervention rate... that’s about situations where a driver needs to step in for safety. 

Tesla upgraded the vision encoder, the part of the AI that makes sense of what the cameras see. It’s shared with Robotaxi and Optimus, and Tesla says it was trained on millions of internet videos to help it understand more situations and learn more efficiently. A core piece of how the car, the robotaxi and the robot understand the world is now shared.

Then there’s Tesla Reality View.

The familiar gray driving display is now being replaced by a detailed view of the world around the car, created live from a virtual viewpoint above it. Ashok says the same model that drives the car also draws that scene. Arrows show the turns FSD plans to make, and pins show where it wants to park. 

Elon says you can tap a point in that view to tell the car where to go, with turn markers floating overhead like a video game. 

He says, “It’s like GTA" and the new visualization uses less computing power than the old one.
